item.title: Playwright E2E for Next.js: Multi-Browser + Desktop/Mobile Layering
item.description:
Jest is great for functions and APIs, but it cannot verify full user flows like “click a button → navigate → map loads → modal appears.” In our Next.js project, we built a Playwright E2E setup with three desktop browsers + two mobile viewports, organized by Desktop / Mobile directories. This post is a retrospective, not a rewrite of the official docs.

Why Playwright

Compared with tools like Cypress, Playwright fit our needs especially well:

item.title: From a Frontend Database Architecture to Gradual SSR Migration
item.description:
Our Original Architecture

Early on, the project used a frontend database + backend sync model.

When a user opened the site, data was synced from the backend into a local browser database (IndexedDB / Dexie). After that, almost every read on the page went through this local layer instead of hitting the API on each navigation.

The upside was clear: the first load was slow, but everything after that felt very fast. Lists, detail views, filters, and sorting were essentially local reads with almost no network latency—closer to an offline-first web app than a classic SPA.

item.title: How to Display Custom Navigation Routes on Google Maps Using the Google Maps JavaScript API
item.description:
1. Background

When using the Google Maps JavaScript API, there may be scenarios where users need to query routes. In such cases, how can navigation routes be displayed on the map?

2. Related Concepts

With the Google Directions API, you can retrieve navigation information between two or more locations — such as distance, duration, and route details on the map. By passing this data to the Maps JavaScript API, it’s possible to render the navigation route directly on an embedded map.
